growth_story.headline: Bhutan's growth has risen and fallen with its dams: 6.9 percent a year in 2002–2011, 3.3 since 2012, and new plants now lift income per person to a peak.
growth_story.arc: Bhutan's income per person grew 4.8 percent a year in 1990–2001, in an economy that had exported hydropower since the Chukha plant opened in 1988. Growth sped up to 6.9 percent a year in 2002–2011, when fixed investment reached 68.9 percent of GDP in 2004 and the Tala plant was built; the year it opened, 2007, was the era's best at 14.8 percent. Since 2012 growth has averaged 3.3 percent a year: curbs to stop a shortage of Indian rupees halted building and services in 2012, geology held up the Punatsangchhu-I dam, and income per person fell 10.8 percent in the 2020 pandemic. Large-scale emigration slowed the recovery in 2023, but new hydropower and capital spending lifted growth to 6.8 percent in 2024 and 7.3 percent in 2025. Income per person is now at its highest level, yet the last decade's average of 3.2 percent a year is well below the 6.2 of the decade before.

threads.title: Dams as the engine
threads.text: Bhutan's large-scale power exports began with the Chukha plant in 1988, and big plants have made growth swing ever since. When the Tala plant opened in 2007, income per person grew 14.8 percent, the best year of the 2002–2011 era.

threads.title: The 2012 rupee squeeze
threads.text: Building plants and importing for them drained Bhutan's holdings of Indian rupees. In 2012 the authorities brought in measures to stop the shortage, and construction and services stalled, which opened the slower era that has run since.

threads.title: Delayed dams and costly inputs
threads.text: Hydropower building kept investment high after 2012, but the Punatsangchhu-I dam ran into geological problems early and is still held up. In 2026 higher diesel costs have also raised the cost of hydropower and government projects.

threads.text: Growth picked up to 6.8 percent in 2024 and 7.3 percent in 2025, and the IMF counts the opening of major hydropower plants among the drivers, alongside grant-financed public investment. The World Bank ties the near-term outlook to the Punatsangchhu-II plant running at full capacity.

growth_story.tension: The sources present hydropower building as the engine of growth, yet the slowest era, 2012–2025 at 3.3 percent a year, came while fixed investment stayed high: 69.2 percent of GDP in 2012 and still 42.1 percent in 2024. The IMF also calls growth in 2023 subdued and links the weak recovery to large-scale emigration, but income per person still grew 3.9 percent that year: people leaving shrinks the population base, so the per-person measure can look steadier than the economy itself.
